title: Telegram agent: end-to-end architecture
prompt: Walk me through the architecture of your Telegram assistant. What happens from the moment you send a message until the reply appears?
answer: Reference points: a Bun/TypeScript long-poll poller runs 24/7 on a DigitalOcean VPS as a systemd service (journald logs, Restart=always). Incoming message -> allowlist check -> a 3.5s debounce window batches rapid bursts into one turn. Each turn spawns a fresh `claude -p` (Claude Code CLI) with a prompt assembled from per-chat history, BM25-recalled past messages (SQLite FTS5), guarded long-term memory, and relevant skills. The CLI's stream-json stdout is parsed incrementally and throttle-edited into the Telegram message (~1.5s edits, 4096-char overflow splits). State lives in SQLite plus small JSON files written atomically (tmp+rename). Side systems: reminders/[AUTO] jobs, iCloud CalDAV calendar+tasks, monitors, and the daily quiz all hang off the same poller loop.

title: Telegram agent: why a fresh process per message?
prompt: Your bot spawns a fresh LLM CLI process for every message instead of keeping one long-running session. Defend that decision. What are the tradeoffs?
answer: Reference points: isolation (a hung or crashed turn dies alone under its own timeout and can never poison the main loop), per-message model routing (cheap fast model by default, /opus escalation per message), least-privilege per session type (scheduled [AUTO] jobs run with a restricted tool surface), and config freshness (CLAUDE.md and memory are re-read every turn, so most behavior changes deploy without a restart). Continuity is rebuilt deliberately: injected history, recall, and memory instead of implicit context accumulation. Costs: cold-start latency per message and no free in-context continuity; both acceptable for a personal-assistant load profile.

title: Telegram agent: safety for an LLM with shell access
prompt: The assistant's LLM can run shell commands on its own server. How do you make destructive or outward-facing actions safe?
answer: Reference points, defense in depth: (1) a PreToolUse guard hook with a hardline command blocklist, fail-closed even in full-permission mode, which also blocks edits to the guard/hook/env files themselves; (2) confirm-before-write: risky writes (calendar, deletions) are frozen as proposals and executed only when the user taps an inline approve button, one execution path; (3) capability absence: the Gmail connector has no send tool, so 'never send email' is enforced by architecture, not prompt; (4) untrusted-content quarantine: facts or procedures learned from emails/web/files are held back until explicitly approved; (5) secret redaction at the single send chokepoint; (6) a chat-id allowlist in front of everything.

title: Telegram agent: safe self-modification
prompt: Your bot can edit its own source code on the server it runs on. How did you design self-modification so a deploy can never lose or silently ship unreviewed code?
answer: Reference points: the agent's policy is commit-to-a-branch, never hot-patch main. Its origin remote is deliberately credential-less, so it physically cannot push; a human fetches the branch straight off the server over ssh, reviews it on a desktop, and lands it as a normal PR. deploy.sh captures any uncommitted tracked edits to an autosave branch before running git reset --hard, so a deploy cannot destroy self-written code. The guard hook blocks the agent from editing the guard itself, the hook files, or the env. Real examples to tell: the message-debounce feature and a default-model upgrade were both written by the agent on the server, rescued, reviewed (and fixed), then merged.

title: Telegram agent: streaming replies without a streaming API
prompt: Telegram has no streaming API. How do your replies still stream in live like ChatGPT?
answer: Reference points: the CLI emits stream-json events on stdout; the poller parses them incrementally and edits a placeholder message in place via editMessageText, throttled to ~1.5s so Telegram's rate limits are respected. Overflow past Telegram's 4096-char limit rolls into follow-up messages. A typing indicator and emoji reaction acknowledge receipt before the first token. The stream parser is a separate tested module (stream.ts); partial output is preserved if a turn is stopped mid-stream with /stop.

title: Telegram agent: the message debounce
prompt: What is the message-debounce feature in your bot, why does it exist, and why is the window 3.5 seconds?
answer: Reference points: people send one thought as several rapid messages; without batching, each spawns its own LLM turn that answers a fragment. A quiet-window debounce buffers messages and flushes them as ONE combined turn. The window resets on every arrival, so it measures the gap between messages, not total typing time. It started at 2s and was widened to 3.5s from real usage (iPhone typing gaps between sends). The interesting engineering was the seams: the shutdown drain flushes the buffer so a deploy can't eat messages, /stop clears it, quiz commands are handled in code and must not leak into a batched prompt, and the allowlist is checked per sender, not per batch.

title: Telegram agent: memory that resists prompt injection
prompt: How does your assistant's long-term memory work, and how do you stop prompt-injected 'facts' from an email or web page from poisoning it?
answer: Reference points: core facts live in SQLite and are injected into every prompt. Writes are guarded by provenance: facts the user states are active immediately; anything derived from outside content (email, web, files) is quarantined and unused until the user explicitly promotes it. Entries are threat-scanned on write, size budgets force consolidation instead of unbounded growth, and every change lands in an audit journal with soft-delete. Retrieval over the full chat archive is BM25/FTS5 keyword search, a deliberate no-embeddings choice: simpler, debuggable, and good enough for one user's history.

title: Telegram agent: Hebrew, English, and BiDi rendering
prompt: Your bot replies in Hebrew, which is right-to-left. What breaks when English tokens are mixed into RTL text, and how did you solve it?
answer: Reference points: the Unicode BiDi algorithm can visually reorder mixed-direction lines; the worst offender is an English term followed by an em-dash or colon then Hebrew, which reliably scrambles. The fix is rules baked into the bot's system prompt: never separate scripts with a dash/colon, put standalone LTR tokens (URLs, file paths, commands) on their own lines, give each language its own line when explaining, and never end an RTL sentence with a bare LTR token. This came from a real rendering bug report and is a good story about localization details that unit tests don't catch.

title: Telegram agent: a production incident
prompt: Tell me about a production incident on your Telegram assistant and how you debugged it. (Answer in STAR form.)
answer: Pick one real incident and STAR it. Strong options: (1) the two-pollers war: the tmux-run poller died silently and took its logs; after migrating to systemd, any second poller instance caused Telegram 409 conflicts, so the rule became exactly one consumer of getUpdates, verified with a kill-test. (2) The deploy that ate a button press: restarts dropped consumed-but-unprocessed updates; fixed with graceful drain (SIGTERM stops fetching, drains queues up to 80s, then exits), diagnosed via offset-file mtime and pending_update_count forensics. (3) Auth expiry: the CLI's OAuth token expired after ~28h causing 401s; fixed with a long-lived token in the service env plus a runbook.

title: Telegram agent: saying no to a feature
prompt: Tell me about a time you deliberately cut scope or said no to a capability on this project, and why.
answer: Reference stories: (1) Email sending: chose drafts-only. The connector deliberately has no send tool, so the bot composes a draft, the user approves it in chat, the draft lands in Gmail, and the human presses Send. Turning 'the bot could send email' from a risk into an architectural impossibility was worth more than the feature. (2) LLM-based message routing: rejected a per-message classifier call because it would re-pay CLI startup latency on every message; shipped cheap keyword/prefix routing instead. The theme to land: on an agent with real-world side effects, the safest capability is one that structurally does not exist.

title: Telegram agent: hardest tradeoff
prompt: What is the hardest architectural tradeoff you made on the Telegram assistant, and would you decide differently today?
answer: No single right answer; strong candidates: (1) fresh process per message vs a persistent LLM session (isolation and routing vs latency and rebuilt continuity); (2) long-polling vs webhooks (simplicity on one small VPS vs instant delivery and horizontal scale); (3) SQLite + small JSON state files vs one proper database (transparent, atomic-rename simple, but state is scattered); (4) no embeddings, BM25 only (debuggable, but semantic recall is weaker). A good answer names the constraint that drove the choice (single user, single small VPS, safety-first) and states what threshold would flip the decision.

title: Telegram agent: scaling from 1 user to 100
prompt: The assistant serves one user today. What would you change to serve 100 users safely?
answer: Reference points: switch long-poll to webhooks behind a small HTTP service; shard state per user (history, memory, quiz, reminders) instead of global files; per-chat serialized queues with global concurrency limits on LLM spawns; per-user auth and secrets (each user's own connector tokens), turning the allowlist into a real identity model; per-user quotas to bound cost; observability (structured logs, per-user usage metrics, alerting); and a hard look at the guard model, because 100 users means 100 sources of prompt injection against shared infrastructure. Bonus: the confirm-button and quarantine patterns already generalize per user.

title: certimanager: end-to-end architecture
prompt: Walk me through the architecture of certimanager, your certification-tracking SaaS.
answer: Reference points: a Hebrew-language, RTL-first web app for a manager overseeing ~150 field employees with time-limited certifications. Next.js 16 App Router + React 19 frontend styled with Tailwind v4; Supabase supplies Postgres, Auth, and Storage (certification images). middleware.ts gates every /dashboard route behind auth; Supabase access goes through separate client and server factories (SSR-safe). Feature areas: employee CRUD, certification CRUD with image upload, cert-type management, course-candidates with a promotion flow, bulk Excel import, tasks, reports/timeline, and an in-app feedback inbox. Deployed on Render with auto-deploy from master; Vitest unit tests (507 passing) plus Playwright e2e and a staging smoke test.

title: certimanager: multi-tenancy in two layers
prompt: How does multi-tenancy work in certimanager, and why did you implement it in two layers?
answer: Reference points: every query scopes rows by manager_id = auth.uid(). The application layer is the first line: every server action and page-level fetch includes the filter explicitly. Supabase Row Level Security is the second line: policies enforce the same predicate inside Postgres, so a forgotten filter in app code fails closed at the database instead of leaking another tenant's data. The discipline: when adding any new data access, check both places. This is a textbook defense-in-depth story: the DB guarantees isolation, the app layer keeps queries efficient and intent explicit.

title: certimanager: schema evolution with migrations
prompt: How do you evolve certimanager's database schema safely while a real user depends on it?
answer: Reference points: a base schema.sql plus ~20 incremental, numbered migration files applied strictly in order. New requirements never edit the base schema; they land as a new migration, so any environment (fresh local setup, staging, production) reaches the same state by replaying the sequence. Local setup is reproducible: create a Supabase project, run the schema in the SQL editor, apply migrations. The talking point: migrations-as-append-only-log is what makes a solo project safe to change months later, and it pairs with the test suite as the deploy gate.

title: certimanager: design the expiry-notification system
prompt: certimanager tracks expiry dates but push notifications (WhatsApp/SMS/mail) are not built yet. Design that system.
answer: Reference points for a strong answer: a scheduled job (cron or Supabase scheduled/edge function) scans certifications entering configurable windows (30/14/7/0 days); a notifications state table records what was already sent per certification+threshold so alerts are idempotent and fire once; a channel abstraction (mail first, WhatsApp/SMS via a provider like Twilio later) with per-manager preferences; templates in Hebrew with correct RTL; timezone-correct date math; retries with backoff and a dead-letter log for failed sends; and a digest mode (one morning summary vs per-cert spam). Bonus points: cost control per channel and an unsubscribe/quiet-hours policy.

title: certimanager: why Supabase?
prompt: Why did you pick Supabase for certimanager instead of building your own backend, and what are the tradeoffs?
answer: Reference points: as a solo developer with a real user waiting, managed Postgres + Auth + Storage + RLS bought product velocity: no auth service to write, no file-storage plumbing, SQL-first with real migrations instead of an ORM lock-in. The client uses only the anon/public key and RLS is the security model; the service-role key never ships to the browser. Tradeoffs to name honestly: vendor coupling (auth and RLS idioms are Supabase-shaped), RLS policies add a second place where authorization logic lives, and local/offline development needs more setup than a plain SQLite app.

title: certimanager: the Excel bulk import
prompt: How does the Excel bulk import work in certimanager, and what makes importing real-world spreadsheets hard?
answer: Reference points: a dedicated parser module (lib/excel-parser.ts) turns the manager's xlsx files into employees plus certifications. The hard parts are all real-world messiness: inconsistent headers, date cells that arrive as strings/serials in mixed formats (ISO date-formatting fixes were real bugs), duplicate rows needing dedup, and partially-filled records. The honest engineering story: the format ultimately has to match the actual files the real manager uses, which needs a working session with him; until then the import is built against samples with validation before anything is committed to the database.

title: certimanager: testing strategy
prompt: What is your testing strategy on certimanager, and why does it look like that?
answer: Reference points: three layers. Vitest unit tests (507 passing) cover parsing, date logic, and helpers; Playwright end-to-end tests drive real flows in a browser; and a staging smoke test runs against a deployed environment. The whole suite runs in about 80 seconds via one command (npm run test:all), which matters: a solo maintainer only keeps running tests that are fast. Deploys ride Render auto-deploy from master, so the suite is effectively the deploy gate. The talking point: with one developer and a real user, tests are not bureaucracy, they are the only reviewer.

title: certimanager: the auth flow
prompt: Describe certimanager's authentication flow from login to a protected dashboard page render.
answer: Reference points: Supabase Auth manages users (the first account is created from the Supabase dashboard, deliberate for a closed system with no self-signup). Login exchanges credentials for a session persisted in cookies. middleware.ts intercepts every /dashboard request and redirects unauthenticated visitors to login: one chokepoint instead of per-page checks. Server components and server actions get their own Supabase server client (cookie-aware factory) so SSR reads run as the logged-in user, which is also what makes RLS's auth.uid() correct on the server side. Client components use a separate browser-client factory.

title: certimanager: building for a real user
prompt: certimanager has a real user, a manager of ~150 field employees. Tell me how working with a real user shaped the product.
answer: Reference stories: the course-candidates promotion flow exists because his actual process is 'send people to a course, then certify them', not just CRUD; the in-app feedback inbox exists so he can report issues from the field without leaving the app; the Excel import is shaped around his real spreadsheets and honestly still needs a sit-down with his actual files; a mobile bug (a dropdown needing a second tap) surfaced only because he uses it from the field on a phone; and the whole UI is Hebrew-first RTL because that's who uses it. The theme: requirements came from his workflow, and several backlog items are literally his words.

title: certimanager: a bug that reached the user
prompt: Tell me about a bug in certimanager that reached the real user, and how you handled it. (STAR form.)
answer: Reference candidates to STAR: (1) date-format bugs: dates parsed or displayed inconsistently (ISO formatting fixes are in the recent history), risky in an app whose whole point is expiry dates; the fix included normalizing formats and unit tests around date handling. (2) The mobile dropdown that needed a second tap, reported from field usage, likely an event/hydration quirk; fixed and pending verification on his device. A strong close: what changed systemically, i.e. tests added around the fixed area and the in-app feedback inbox shortening the report-to-fix loop.

title: certimanager: running a product solo
prompt: You are the product manager, developer, QA, and support for certimanager. How do you keep that sustainable?
answer: Reference points: a backlog fed by user meetings and the in-app feedback inbox, so priorities come from real usage, not guesses; incremental numbered migrations so schema changes months apart stay safe; a fast three-layer test suite (unit, e2e, staging smoke, ~80s) acting as the reviewer; Render auto-deploy from master so shipping is push-and-watch; and honest deferral: features that need the user's input (the real xlsx formats, notification channels) are parked as open questions instead of guessed at. 317 commits of steady small increments rather than big-bang rewrites.

title: Your two resume projects, compared
prompt: Compare your two main projects, the Telegram agent and certimanager. Where do their architectures differ and why, and what do they share?
answer: Reference points: they solve opposite problems. certimanager is a classic multi-tier SaaS: browser frontend, managed Postgres backend, and the core risk is data isolation, answered with two-layer tenancy (app filter + RLS). The Telegram agent is a long-running stateful service wrapping an LLM CLI, where the core risk is an AI taking real-world actions, answered with guard hooks, confirm buttons, capability absence, and quarantined memory. Different delivery too: Render auto-deploy vs a VPS with systemd and a rescue-aware deploy script. Shared DNA: TypeScript, tests as the deploy gate (594 and 507 tests), small incremental changes, Hebrew/RTL first-class, and both serve one real demanding user.

Output: 4

lc_description:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi] represent the start and the end of the ith interval and intervals is sorted in ascending order by starti. You are also given an interval newInterval = [start, end] that represents the start and end of another interval.

Insert newInterval into intervals such that intervals is still sorted in ascending order by starti and intervals still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

Return intervals after the insertion.

Note that you don't need to modify intervals in-place. You can make a new array and return it.

Example 1:

Input: intervals = [[1,3],[6,9]], newInterval = [2,5]
Output: [[1,5],[6,9]]

Example 2:

Input: intervals = [[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]], newInterval = [4,8]
Output: [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]]
Explanation: Because the new interval [4,8] overlaps with [3,5],[6,7],[8,10].

Constraints:

	- 0 <= intervals.length <= 104

	- intervals[i].length == 2

	- 0 <= starti <= endi <= 105

	- intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.

	- newInterval.length == 2

	- 0 <= start <= end <= 105

title: When to use Bitwise XOR
prompt: When do you use the Bitwise XOR pattern? What are the two key XOR identities you must remember?
answer: Use XOR for problems where pairs cancel and a singleton remains: single number in 1..N, find missing number, find two non-repeating numbers (separate by a set bit). Identities: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a. XOR is commutative and associative — order of XORs doesn't matter. O(n) time, O(1) space.
hint: What does a ^ a equal? || How do you separate two unique numbers from a pile of pairs? || Why is XOR commutative so important here?

title: When to use Top K Elements
prompt: When do you use the Top K Elements pattern? Why a heap of size K and not a full sort?
answer: Use Top K for 'find the K largest/smallest/frequent' problems. Push elements into a min-heap; when size exceeds K, pop the smallest. At the end, the heap holds the top K. Time: O(n log K) — beats sort's O(n log n) for K << n. For 'frequent' variants, first count with a hash map, then heap by count.
hint: Why a MIN-heap to find the K LARGEST? || What's left in the heap at the end? || What's the time complexity vs sorting the full array?

title: When to use K-way Merge
prompt: When do you use the K-way Merge pattern? Walk through merging K sorted lists.
answer: Use K-way Merge whenever the input is K sorted lists/arrays/streams: merge K lists, smallest range covering K lists, K-th smallest in a sorted matrix. Push the head of each list into a min-heap. Pop the smallest, append to the output, push its successor. Time: O(N log K) where N = total elements.
hint: How big is the heap at any moment? || Why is this O(N log K) instead of O(N log N)? || What happens when one of the K lists is exhausted?

title: When to use 0/1 Knapsack (DP)
prompt: When do you use the 0/1 Knapsack DP pattern? Sketch the transition.
answer: Use 0/1 Knapsack for problems that pick each item at most once to satisfy a target: subset sum, partition equal subset, target sum, count of subsets. dp[i][c] = best value using first i items with capacity c. Transition: dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c-w_i] + v_i). Can be space-optimized to 1D by iterating c from high to low.
hint: Why iterate capacity from HIGH to LOW in the 1D version? || What two states do you compare at each cell? || What's the unbounded-knapsack variant's difference?

title: When to use Topological Sort
prompt: When do you use Topological Sort? What graph property does it require?
answer: Use Topological Sort for ordering problems with dependencies: course schedule, build order, task scheduling, alien dictionary. Requires a DAG (no cycles). Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, queue zero-in-degree nodes, pop and decrement neighbors' in-degrees, repeat. If you process fewer than N nodes, there's a cycle. O(V + E).
hint: What kind of graph does it require? || What does it mean if you can't process all nodes? || What initial set seeds the queue?

title: Pattern: sliding-window
prompt: You're given an array of integers and need to find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size K. Which pattern applies?
answer: Sliding Window. Signals: 'contiguous subarray' + 'fixed size K'. Slide a window of width K, maintain the running sum by adding the new right and subtracting the old left.
hint: Look at the words 'contiguous' and 'size K'. || What can you reuse between consecutive windows? || What's the total time complexity?

title: Pattern: two-pointers
prompt: Given a sorted array, find a pair of indices whose values sum to a target. Which pattern applies?
answer: Two Pointers. Sorted + pair-sum is the canonical signal. Move left right when the sum is too small, move right left when too big.
hint: Sorted array — what does that buy you? || If the sum is too big, which pointer moves? || Could you do it with a hash set? Yes — but two pointers is O(1) space.

title: Pattern: fast-and-slow-pointers
prompt: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the list has a cycle (without using extra memory). Which pattern applies?
answer: Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's cycle). Two pointers, slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. If they ever meet, there's a cycle. O(1) extra space.
hint: What's special about a fast pointer in a cyclic list? || Can a hash set work? Yes — but it's O(n) space. || What's the relative speed?

title: Pattern: merge-intervals
prompt: Merge a collection of meeting time ranges that overlap. Which pattern applies?
answer: Merge Intervals. Sort by start time, then sweep: if current.start ≤ prev.end, extend prev.end; else push current. O(n log n).
hint: What's the very first step on the unsorted input? || What's the overlap condition? || What invariant do you maintain about the output?

title: Pattern: cyclic-sort
prompt: Given an array of size N containing numbers from 1..N with exactly one number missing, find the missing number — in O(1) extra space. Which pattern applies?
answer: Cyclic Sort. Because values are in range 1..N, you can place each at its index. The index whose value doesn't match is the missing number. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
hint: What constraint on the values is the giveaway? || Could you XOR? Yes — but cyclic sort generalises better. || How do you put value v at its correct index?

title: Pattern: top-k-elements
prompt: Find the K-th largest element in a stream of integers where new numbers keep arriving. Which pattern applies?
answer: Top K Elements with a min-heap of size K. Pushes are O(log K); reading the K-th largest is the heap top in O(1). Beats sorting the whole stream.
hint: Min-heap or max-heap for K LARGEST? || What's in the heap at the end? || Why is this O(n log K) and not O(n log n)?

title: Pattern: k-way-merge
prompt: You have K sorted lists. Find the smallest range that includes at least one number from each list. Which pattern applies?
answer: K-way Merge with a min-heap of K elements (one head per list). Track the current max across heads; the smallest valid range is found by repeatedly popping the min and pushing its successor.

title: Pattern: two-heaps
prompt: Find the median of a stream of numbers — supporting both insert and get-median operations efficiently. Which pattern applies?
answer: Two Heaps. A max-heap holds the lower half and a min-heap holds the upper half; insert into the right side and rebalance to keep size difference ≤ 1. Median is O(1), insert is O(log n).

title: Pattern: topological-sort
prompt: Schedule courses with prerequisites — return any valid ordering, or detect that none exists. Which pattern applies?
answer: Topological Sort (Kahn's algorithm). Build in-degrees from prerequisites, queue all zero-in-degree courses, pop and decrement neighbors. If you process fewer than N, there's a cycle (impossible).

title: Pattern: 01-knapsack-dp
prompt: Given a set of positive integers, determine if it can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sum. Which pattern applies?
answer: 0/1 Knapsack DP. The total sum must be even; then ask: can a subset sum to total/2? dp[i][c] = is it possible to get sum c using the first i items? Each item is included or not — classic 0/1.

title: Load Balancing
prompt: Design the load balancing layer for a high-traffic web service. What algorithms would you choose, where would the load balancer sit, and how do you handle health checks and sticky sessions?
answer: Layer 4 (TCP) LBs (HAProxy, NLB) — fast, no payload inspection. Layer 7 (HTTP) LBs (Nginx, ALB, Envoy) — content-aware routing, header rewrites, SSL termination. Algorithms: Round Robin (uniform backends), Weighted RR (heterogeneous), Least Connections (long-lived requests), Consistent Hashing (sticky cache locality, minimal disruption on scale). Health checks: active (HTTP /health every N seconds) + passive (track per-connection errors). Sticky sessions: cookie-based affinity or consistent hash on user id — but prefer stateless backends so any node can serve any request. Place the LB in front of every horizontally-scalable tier (web, app, cache).
hint: L4 vs L7 — what does each see? || Why is consistent hashing nicer than mod-N hashing for cache? || What's the trade-off of sticky sessions?

title: Caching Strategies
prompt: Describe the main caching strategies (cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back). Where would a CDN, an in-memory cache like Redis, and the database fit in?
answer: Cache-aside (lazy): app checks cache, falls through to DB on miss, populates cache. Simple but stale risk on writes. Read-through: cache itself fetches from DB on miss — encapsulates cache logic. Write-through: every write goes to cache and DB synchronously — consistent but slower writes. Write-back: write to cache, async-flush to DB — fastest writes but risk of data loss on cache crash. Layers: browser cache → CDN (edge, geo-distributed static + dynamic) → API gateway → in-memory cache (Redis, Memcached) → DB. Invalidation strategies: TTL (simplest), explicit invalidate on write, versioned keys (no invalidation needed). Hard problem: cache stampede on key expiry — use lock or stale-while-revalidate.
hint: Which strategy is best when stale data is unacceptable? || Where does write-back lose data? || What's a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?

title: Choosing SQL vs NoSQL
prompt: How do you decide between SQL (relational) and NoSQL for a new service? Compare the major NoSQL families (document, key-value, column-family, graph) and when each shines.
answer: SQL (Postgres, MySQL): strong consistency, ACID transactions, joins, ad-hoc queries, schema enforcement. Choose when relationships matter, transactions are critical (finance, inventory), or queries are exploratory. NoSQL families: Document (MongoDB, DynamoDB) — flexible schemas, denormalised aggregates, great for content/profile data. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) — extreme write/read throughput, simple lookup keys, session storage. Column-family (Cassandra, ScyllaDB) — write-heavy time-series, multi-DC replication, eventual consistency. Graph (Neo4j) — many-to-many traversal-heavy workloads (social, fraud). Choose based on access pattern, scale (horizontal vs vertical), consistency tolerance, and team familiarity. Polyglot persistence is fine — pick per service.
hint: What does 'access pattern' mean for a NoSQL choice? || Which family handles writes per second best? || When is a graph DB actually warranted vs SQL with indexes?

title: Database Sharding
prompt: Walk through how you would shard a write-heavy relational database. What shard-key strategies exist, and what are the operational pitfalls?
answer: Sharding partitions data horizontally across N nodes; each shard owns a slice. Strategies: Range-based (e.g. user_id 1–1M on shard A) — simple, supports range scans, but hotspots if data is skewed. Hash-based (hash(user_id) % N) — uniform distribution, no range scans across shards. Consistent hashing — minimises data movement when N changes (cache & DynamoDB use this). Geographic (by region) — latency wins but cross-region joins are painful. Directory/lookup table — flexible but adds a hop. Pitfalls: cross-shard joins (avoid via denormalisation or app-side joins), distributed transactions (avoid; use sagas or single-shard transactions), rebalancing (consistent hashing helps), hot shard (re-shard or split). Always have a plan for shard migrations from day one.
hint: What's wrong with mod-N hashing when you grow the cluster? || What's the cost of a cross-shard transaction? || How do you keep a related set of rows on the same shard?

title: Message Queues and Async Processing
prompt: When do you reach for a message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) instead of synchronous HTTP between services? Compare the major options.
answer: Use a queue when: producer and consumer have different rates, work must survive a consumer crash, you want to decouple services, or you need to fan out one event to many consumers. Synchronous HTTP between services creates tight coupling and cascading failures. Options: Kafka — append-only log, high throughput, replayable, multiple consumer groups; great for event sourcing, streaming analytics. RabbitMQ — flexible routing (topics, fanout, direct), per-message ack, classic work queue. SQS — managed, simple FIFO/standard, no ordering guarantee in standard mode. NATS / Redis Streams — lighter, lower-latency, less durability by default. Patterns: at-least-once with idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues for poison messages, backpressure via consumer-side concurrency caps.
hint: What does 'replayable' mean and which broker gives you that? || Why do consumers need to be idempotent? || What's a dead-letter queue for?

title: CAP and PACELC
prompt: Explain the CAP theorem and its extension PACELC. Walk through a real example of each kind of choice.
answer: CAP: in a distributed system, during a network Partition you must choose Consistency or Availability. You can never sacrifice partition tolerance in practice — networks fail. CP systems (Mongo with majority writes, HBase, Zookeeper, etcd): refuse writes during partition to keep data consistent. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB default, Couchbase): keep accepting writes during partition, may return stale data. PACELC adds the no-partition case: Else, choose between Latency and Consistency. PA/EL (DynamoDB default) — fast, eventually consistent. PC/EC (HBase, traditional RDBMS) — slower, always strongly consistent. PA/EC and PC/EL also exist. Real example: a shopping cart prefers AP (always accept items); a bank ledger prefers CP (better to reject than double-spend).
hint: Why is P 'mandatory' in any real distributed system? || What does PACELC add over CAP? || Pick AP vs CP for: shopping cart, bank ledger, DNS, leader election.

title: Rate Limiting
prompt: Design a rate limiter for an API gateway serving millions of users. Which algorithm would you use, and where would the counter live?
answer: Algorithms: Token Bucket — refill at rate R, burst up to B; smooth limits with controlled bursts; used by AWS API Gateway, Stripe. Leaky Bucket — fixed output rate, queue absorbs bursts; great for smoothing. Fixed Window Counter — simple but boundary spikes (e.g. 100/min from 23:59:59 + 100/min from 00:00:01). Sliding Window Log — exact, but memory-heavy. Sliding Window Counter — weighted blend of two adjacent windows, good middle ground. Storage: Redis with atomic INCR + EXPIRE per (user, route, window) — fast and shared across gateway nodes. Decision flow: per-user limit, per-IP fallback for anonymous, distinguish authenticated tiers. Return 429 with Retry-After header. Don't over-rely on client-side enforcement.
hint: Token bucket vs leaky bucket — what's the difference in burst behaviour? || Why is a fixed window prone to boundary spikes? || Where should the counter live for a multi-node gateway?

title: URL Shortener
prompt: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly). Cover the encoding scheme, storage, read/write paths, and how to scale to billions of links.
answer: Encoding: base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z) → 6 chars = 56 billion uniques; or distributed-id (Snowflake) and base62-encode it. Avoid raw hashes — collisions and unpredictable length. Storage: key-value (DynamoDB / Cassandra) keyed on the short code, with a backref index on long URL for dedup. Write path: generate id (counter sharded by region, or Snowflake), encode, write, return. Cache the new mapping. Read path: cache (Redis with high hit rate, since reads dominate ~100:1), fall back to DB, 301 redirect (cacheable) or 302 (analytics-friendly). Scale: read-heavy → CDN-cache redirects, scale DB read replicas, partition by hash of short code. Analytics: async pipeline (Kafka → S3 → batch). TTL: optional per-link expiry. Custom slugs: validate uniqueness, reserve namespace.
hint: Why is base62 a sensible default? || What's the read-to-write ratio and what does it imply? || 301 vs 302 for redirects?

title: News Feed (Twitter/Facebook style)
prompt: Design a personalised news feed at Twitter/Instagram scale. Compare the fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read trade-off and how you'd handle celebrities.
answer: Two extremes — Fanout on write (push): when user U posts, push the post id into every follower's feed list (Redis sorted set per user). Reads are fast (O(N) over a precomputed list); writes are expensive if U has 10M followers. Fanout on read (pull): on each feed read, query the latest from each followee and merge. Reads are expensive; writes are cheap. Hybrid (best in practice): push for normal users; pull for celebrities (a per-user follower threshold flips the strategy). Feed-storage = Redis sorted set capped at ~1k entries. Ranking: separate scoring service combines recency, affinity, content signals. Hot path: precomputed feed list + cache; cold path: regenerate on demand. Use a queue (Kafka) for fanout writes so the write path stays sub-100ms.
hint: Why does fanout-on-write break for celebrities? || What's the read-vs-write trade-off? || Where do you cap a feed's stored length and why?

title: Real-time Chat (WhatsApp-style)
prompt: Design a real-time chat system supporting 1:1 and group messaging at scale. Cover transport, message storage, delivery guarantees, and presence.
answer: Transport: persistent WebSocket connection to a stateless gateway tier; the gateway routes messages via a pub/sub layer (Kafka or Redis pub/sub) keyed by user id. Storage: per-conversation message log in Cassandra/DynamoDB (partition by conversation_id, clustered by timestamp), with a read-receipts table separately. Delivery: at-least-once with idempotent client ids → exactly-once UX. Track per-recipient delivered/seen timestamps. Groups: maintain a group→members table; on message, fan out a notification to each online member's gateway, and persist for offline retrieval (push notification on top). Presence: heartbeat through the WebSocket; coarse-grained (online/offline) is enough for most UIs, fine-grained 'last seen' is a separate write throttled to a minute. Scale: shard by user_id, sticky WS routing via consistent hashing.
hint: Why WebSocket and not HTTP polling? || How do you achieve exactly-once UX with at-least-once delivery? || Where does the message live for an offline user?

title: Consistent Hashing
prompt: Explain consistent hashing. Why is it preferred over mod-N hashing for distributed caches and storage?
answer: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a virtual ring (hash space 0..2^64-1). Each key is owned by the next node clockwise on the ring. Adding or removing one node only re-maps the keys that fall between the new/removed node and its predecessor — about 1/N of keys. Mod-N hashing remaps almost all keys when N changes (catastrophic for caches). Real-world: use 'virtual nodes' (each physical node owns hundreds of points on the ring) to smooth distribution and avoid hotspots. Used by Amazon DynamoDB, Cassandra, memcached clients, content-addressable storage. Trade-offs: more complex than mod-N, requires a ring-aware client or a coordinator that knows the mapping.
hint: What fraction of keys move when you add the N+1-th node? || Why virtual nodes? || Which famous systems use it?

title: Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)
prompt: What is a CDN, how does it work, and what kinds of content are best served from one? When does a CDN NOT help?
answer: A CDN is a globally distributed network of edge servers that cache content close to users, reducing latency and origin load. How it works: DNS routes the user to the nearest edge (geo-DNS or anycast); the edge serves the cached object if fresh, otherwise pulls from origin (or a regional shield) and caches it. Best for: static assets (JS, CSS, images, video), API responses that can be cached on cache keys (consider Vary: headers), and large file downloads. Push CDN vs Pull CDN: push pre-warms (good for known assets); pull caches on demand (good for long tail). Cache invalidation: purge by URL or use versioned URLs (the only reliable way at scale). CDNs DON'T help: highly personalised content, write-heavy paths, or content where staleness is unacceptable. Major players: Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront, Akamai.
hint: How does the user reach the nearest edge? || Why are versioned URLs the only sane cache invalidation? || What kinds of content does a CDN NOT help with?

title: 8 Scalability Strategies
prompt: Look at the diagram and name the 8 common strategies for scaling a system. For each one — when would you choose it and what is its main trade-off?
answer: 1. Stateless services — remove server-side session state so any node can serve any request (prerequisite for horizontal scaling). 2. Horizontal scaling — add more nodes behind a load balancer instead of upgrading a single machine (unlimited scale, but requires statelessness). 3. Caching — store computed results in Redis/CDN to reduce DB load and latency; trade-off is staleness. 4. Database replication — primary for writes, read replicas for reads; trade-off is eventual consistency on replicas. 5. Database sharding — partition data across nodes by shard key; trade-off is cross-shard joins and hot-shard risk. 6. Async messaging (queues) — decouple producers and consumers via Kafka/SQS; trades latency for throughput and resilience. 7. Event sourcing — store the log of events as truth, derive current state on read; enables replay and audit. 8. Microservices — split by domain so each service scales independently; trade-off is operational complexity and network latency.
hint: Which strategy must come before horizontal scaling can work? || Which strategies reduce database load directly? || What problem does async messaging solve that synchronous calls can't?

title: 10 System Design Trade-offs
prompt: Study the diagram showing 10 key system design trade-offs. Pick any 3 and explain the specific context where you'd choose each side of the trade-off.
answer: Key trade-offs: 1. Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling — vertical is simpler (no distribution needed) but hits a ceiling; horizontal scales indefinitely but requires statelessness. 2. SQL vs NoSQL — SQL for strong consistency and relations; NoSQL for scale and flexible schema. 3. Consistency vs Availability (CAP) — CP for finance (can't lose writes); AP for shopping carts (always accept). 4. Latency vs Throughput — optimize for latency in interactive UIs; throughput in batch/analytics. 5. Read vs Write performance — caching and read replicas improve reads at cost of write complexity; write-ahead log and append-only storage improve writes. 6. Push vs Pull — push (fan-out) is faster for users but costly when a celebrity has 100M followers; pull lets consumers control rate. 7. Strong vs Eventual Consistency — strong for banking; eventual for social feeds. 8. Batch vs Stream — batch is simpler for analytics on historical data; streaming for real-time decisions. 9. Synchronous vs Asynchronous — sync is easier to reason about; async decouples and buffers. 10. Monolith vs Microservices — monolith is simpler to start; microservices scale independently but add ops complexity.
hint: CAP theorem — partition always happens, so pick C or A || When does eventual consistency break down (hint: banking vs social)? || Why does push fan-out not work for celebrity accounts with 100M followers?

title: Database Scaling Cheat Sheet
prompt: The diagram shows 7 strategies for scaling a database. Walk through each one and explain in what order you'd apply them as traffic grows.
answer: Order of operations as scale grows: 1. Indexing — add first, always; eliminates full table scans, nearly free. 2. Caching (Redis) — put in-memory cache in front of DB; absorbs 80%+ of reads for typical apps. 3. Read replicas — offload SELECT queries to replicas; works when read:write ratio is high (>10:1). 4. Vertical scaling — upgrade to a bigger server; buys time but expensive and has a ceiling. 5. Connection pooling (PgBouncer) — multiplexes many app connections to fewer DB connections; critical for Postgres which has per-connection overhead. 6. Sharding — horizontally partition data by shard key (user_id, tenant_id); eliminates single node as bottleneck but complicates cross-shard joins. 7. Multi-primary (active-active) — multiple writable nodes; solves write availability but requires conflict resolution. Apply in this order: indexing → caching → replicas → pooling → vertical → sharding → multi-primary.
hint: Indexing costs almost nothing — why not start there? || What read:write ratio makes replicas worth it? || Why is sharding listed late when it seems powerful?

title: 9 Microservices Best Practices
prompt: Look at the diagram listing 9 microservices best practices. Describe each one and what problem it solves.
answer: 1. Each service owns its database — prevents tight coupling; services can choose the right DB technology (polyglot persistence). 2. Service mesh (Istio/Envoy) — handles inter-service TLS, retries, circuit breaking, and observability at the infrastructure layer so services don't need to implement it. 3. API Gateway — single entry point for clients; handles auth, rate limiting, request routing. 4. Circuit breaker — stops cascading failures; when a downstream service fails, open the circuit and return a fallback quickly. 5. Centralized logging — aggregate logs from all services (ELK stack / Datadog) with a correlation/trace ID per request. 6. Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin) — trace a request across service boundaries; essential for diagnosing latency. 7. Container orchestration (Kubernetes) — deploys, scales, and reschedules containers automatically. 8. Health checks and graceful shutdown — K8s liveness/readiness probes; drain connections before terminating. 9. Event-driven communication — use Kafka/RabbitMQ for async workflows to decouple services and avoid synchronous chains.
hint: What happens if two services share a database? || Why is distributed tracing harder than centralized logging? || What is a cascading failure and how do circuit breakers prevent it?

title: 6 Software Architectural Patterns
prompt: Study the diagram of 6 architectural patterns. Name each pattern, describe how data flows in it, and give an example use case.
answer: 1. Layered (N-tier) — horizontal layers (Presentation → Business → Data); each layer only talks to adjacent layers. Classic web apps. Simple but tight coupling within layers. 2. Event-driven — producers emit events to a bus; consumers subscribe independently. Loose coupling, great for async workflows (order processing). Complexity: debugging and eventual consistency. 3. Microkernel (Plugin) — a small core with pluggable add-ons (IDE plugins, browser extensions). New features don't touch core. 4. Microservices — independently deployable services per domain, each with its own DB. Scales per service but adds operational overhead. 5. Space-based — distributes both processing and storage across nodes to eliminate DB as bottleneck (used in trading platforms and gaming). 6. Event-sourcing + CQRS — store events as the source of truth; read model is a projection. Enables audit log and time-travel debugging. Best for high-write domains with complex business rules.
hint: What's the key difference between event-driven and event-sourcing? || Why does layered architecture still make sense for small teams? || What does 'space-based' solve that microservices don't?

title: 8 REST API Design Tips
prompt: The diagram shows 8 tips for efficient REST API design. List each tip and explain why it matters in production.
answer: 1. Domain-model-driven paths — /users/{id}/orders, not /getUserOrders; maps to resources, not actions. 2. Correct HTTP methods — GET (idempotent read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Using GET for mutations breaks caching and safety semantics. 3. Proper HTTP status codes — 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Error. Never return 200 with an error body. 4. Versioning — /v1/ in path or Accept header; lets you evolve without breaking existing clients. 5. Pagination — cursor-based (stable under inserts) or offset (simpler but skips on concurrent inserts); include next/prev links. 6. Rate limiting — protect backends; return 429 with Retry-After header. 7. Idempotency keys — for POST operations that must not duplicate (payments, orders); client sends a UUID key so retries are safe. 8. Comprehensive error messages — machine-readable error code + human-readable message + details field; helps clients handle errors programmatically.
hint: Why is returning 200 with an error body in the JSON body a bad practice? || What's the difference between 401 and 403? || When does cursor pagination beat offset pagination?

title: Production Web Application Architecture
prompt: The diagram shows the typical architecture of a production web application. Walk through each layer from the user's request to the database, explaining the role of every component.
answer: Request path: 1. DNS — resolves domain to CDN/load balancer IP. 2. CDN — serves static assets (JS, CSS, images) from edge; reduces origin load and latency. 3. Load balancer — distributes traffic across app servers; handles SSL termination, health checks. 4. App servers (stateless) — run business logic; horizontally scalable because state is elsewhere. 5. Cache layer (Redis/Memcached) — stores frequently-read data (sessions, hot DB rows); reduces DB queries. 6. Primary database — write path; SQL for ACID transactions. 7. Read replicas — offload SELECT-heavy workloads from primary. 8. Message queue (Kafka/SQS) — async processing (emails, notifications, analytics); decouples producers from consumers. 9. Worker services — consume from queue; do background jobs (image resizing, PDF generation). 10. Logging and monitoring — aggregate logs and metrics for observability. CI/CD pipeline — automated testing and deployment.
hint: Why must the app servers be stateless? || What does SSL termination at the LB save on the app servers? || What's the difference between the cache layer and CDN caching?

title: 4 Ways Netflix Uses Caching
prompt: Describe 4 ways Netflix uses caching at different layers, and explain the cache invalidation or consistency strategy for each.
answer: 1. CDN edge caching — video chunks and thumbnails cached at 200+ PoPs globally; TTL-based invalidation (chunks are immutable once encoded, thumbnails versioned by URL). 2. API response caching — personalised recommendations and metadata cached in EVCache (Netflix's memcached wrapper); short TTL (~minutes) because recommendations change. 3. Client-side app cache — the Netflix app caches the home screen and recently-watched data locally so the UI feels instant even on poor connections; invalidated on app open or after TTL. 4. Database query cache — frequently-read metadata (movie titles, catalogue) cached in Redis close to the microservice; cache-aside pattern, invalidated on write to DB. Key insight: Netflix separates stable content (video, cached aggressively) from personalised content (cached briefly or not at all) because staleness cost differs.

title: 8 Data Structures Powering Databases
prompt: Look at the diagram listing 8 data structures used by database engines. For each one, explain what it's optimised for and which database or index type uses it.
answer: 1. B-Tree / B+Tree — balanced tree; O(log n) reads and range scans; used by Postgres, MySQL for default indexes. B+Tree keeps data only in leaves, enabling fast sequential range reads. 2. LSM Tree (Log-Structured Merge) — write-optimised; buffered in-memory, flushed to sorted SSTables on disk, compacted in background. Used by Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB. 3. Hash Index — O(1) exact lookup; only equality queries; used by Redis, some Postgres hash indexes. No range queries. 4. SSTable (Sorted String Table) — immutable sorted file written by LSM; enables efficient merge-sort compaction. 5. Skip List — probabilistic ordered structure; O(log n) ops; used by Redis Sorted Sets. 6. Inverted Index — maps terms to document IDs; powers full-text search (Elasticsearch, Postgres tsvector). 7. R-Tree — spatial index; used for geo queries (PostGIS, geospatial DBs). 8. Bloom Filter — probabilistic structure answering 'might exist' / 'definitely not exist'; used in Cassandra and RocksDB to skip disk reads for keys that definitely don't exist.
hint: Why does LSM tree beat B-tree for write-heavy workloads? || What's the false-positive trade-off of a Bloom filter? || Why can't a hash index serve range queries like BETWEEN 100 AND 200?

title: 18 Key OO Design Patterns
prompt: Study the diagram showing OO design patterns grouped by type. Name the 3 groups and at least 2 patterns from each. For each pattern, explain the problem it solves with a one-line example.
answer: Creational (how objects are created): Factory Method — create objects without specifying concrete class (Logger.create('file'|'console')). Singleton — ensure one instance (DB connection pool). Builder — construct complex objects step by step (SQL query builder). Abstract Factory — families of related objects (UI widgets for Windows vs Mac). Prototype — clone an existing object cheaply. Structural (how objects are composed): Adapter — convert one interface to another (legacy payment gateway → modern API). Decorator — add behaviour without subclassing (logging/caching around a service). Proxy — control access to an object (auth proxy, lazy loading). Facade — simplified interface to a complex subsystem. Composite — treat a tree of objects uniformly (file system: folders and files both implement 'size'). Behavioral (how objects communicate): Observer — publish/subscribe; notify listeners on state change (event bus). Strategy — swap algorithms at runtime (sorting strategy). Command — encapsulate a request as an object (undo/redo). Iterator — traverse a collection without exposing its structure. Template Method — define algorithm skeleton, let subclasses fill in steps. Chain of Responsibility — pass request along a handler chain (middleware). State — change behavior based on internal state (order status: pending → paid → shipped).

title: 100X Postgres Scaling at Figma
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Learn how Figma scaled its Postgres database by 100x.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
With 3 million monthly users, Figma’s user base has increased by 200% since 2018.

As a result, its Postgres database witnessed a whopping 100X growth.

*   Vertical Scaling and Replication

    Figma used a single, large Amazon RDS database.

    As a first step, they upgraded to the largest instance available (from r5.12xlarge to r5.24xlarge).

    They also created multiple read replicas to scale read traffic and added PgBouncer as a connection pooler to limit the impact of a growing number of connections.

*   Vertical Partitioning

    The next step was vertical partitioning.

    They migrated high-traffic tables like “Figma Files” and “Organizations” into their separate databases.

    Multiple PgBouncer instances were used to manage the connections for these separate databases.

*   Horizontal Partitioning

    Over time, some tables crossed several terabytes of data and billions of rows.

    Postgres Vacuum became an issue and max IOPS exceeded the limits of Amazon RDS at the time.

    To solve this, Figma implemented horizontal partitioning by splitting large tables across multiple physical databases.

    A new DBProxy service was built to handle routing and query exec

title: 4 Ways of QR Code Payment

Payment through scanning QR code is very common, but do you know how many ways there are to do it?

There are 4 ways, no matter whether you’re using PayPal, Stripe, Paytm, WeChat, or Alipay. Is this surprising to you? To understand this, we will answer two questions.

Who Presents the QR Code?

1.  You can present the QR code, and the merchant scans the code for payment. This is called ‘consumer-presented mode,’ and what the merchant does is direct debit your account.

2.  Obviously, the other way is that the merchant presents the QR code for you to scan to pay the due amount. This is called ‘merchant-presented mode,’ and you grant the direct credit from your account.

Is the QR Code Dynamic or Static?

1.  A dynamic QR code means the QR code will be generated when you present it, or it will automatically regenerate every few seconds. Because it is dynamically generated, it may contain rich information, such as the amount due, transaction type, etc.

2.  A static QR code is generated once and used everywhere. Usually, it only contains the account information.

So there are 2*2=4 ways to scan a QR code, which are:

*   Consumer-presented mode + static QR code
*   Consumer-presented

Designing fault-tolerant systems is crucial for ensuring high availability and reliability in various applications. Here are six top principles of designing fault-tolerant systems:

Replication

Replication involves creating multiple copies of data or services across different nodes or locations.

Redundancy

Redundancy refers to having additional components or systems that can take over in case of a failure.

Load Balancing

Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes a point of failure.

Failover Mechanisms

Failover mechanisms automatically switch to a standby system or component when the primary one fails.

Graceful Degradation

Graceful degradation ensures that a system continues to operate at reduced functionality rather than completely failing when some components fail.

Monitoring and Alerting

Continuously monitor the system's health and performance, and set up alerts for any anomalies or failures.

What is Database Sharding?

Database sharding is a type of database partitioning that separates very large databases into smaller, faster, more easily managed parts called data shards. The word shard means a small piece of something bigger.

Sharding is also known as horizontal partitioning. Each shard contains a portion of the data, and all shards together contain all of the data.

Why Sharding?

Sharding is implemented to solve these problems:

*   Too much data on one machine: A single database server can only handle so much data.

*   Too many requests on one machine: A single database server can only handle so many requests.

*   High Latency: As data grows, query latency increases.

How Sharding Works

Sharding involves splitting a database into multiple, independent parts (shards) and distributing them across different servers or machines. Each shard contains a subset of the data, and all shards collectively hold the entire dataset.

Sharding Key

A sharding key is a column in the database table that determines how the data is distributed across the shards. The sharding key is used by the sharding algorithm to determine which shard a particular row of data should be stored i

title: B-Tree vs. LSM-Tree
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore the differences between B-Tree and LSM-Tree data structures.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
B-Tree

B-Tree is the most widely used indexing data structure in almost all relational databases.

The basic unit of information storage in B-Tree is usually called a “page”. Looking up a key traces down the range of keys until the actual value is found.

LSM-Tree

LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge Tree) is widely used by many NoSQL databases, such as Cassandra, LevelDB, and RocksDB.

LSM-trees maintain key-value pairs and are persisted to disk using a Sorted Strings Table (SSTable), in which the keys are sorted.

Level 0 segments are periodically merged into Level 1 segments. This process is called compaction.

The biggest difference is probably this:

*   B-Tree enables faster reads

*   LSM-Tree enables fast writes

title: Big Endian vs Little Endian
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore big endian vs little endian byte ordering in computer architecture.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
Microprocessor architectures commonly use two different methods to store the individual bytes in memory. This difference is referred to as “byte ordering” or “endian nature”.

Little Endian

Intel x86 processors store a two-byte integer with the least significant byte first, followed by the most significant byte. This is called little-endian byte ordering.

Big Endian

In big endian byte order, the most significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address, and the least significant byte is stored at the highest memory address. Older PowerPC and Motorola 68k architectures often use big endian. In network communications and file storage, we also use big endian.

The byte ordering becomes significant when data is transferred between systems or processed by systems with different endianness. It's important to handle byte order correctly to interpret data consistently across diverse systems.

title: Erasure Coding
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore erasure coding: enhancing data durability in object storage.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
A really cool technique that’s commonly used in object storage such as S3 to improve durability is called Erasure Coding. Let’s take a look at how it works.

Erasure coding deals with data durability differently from replication. It chunks data into smaller pieces (placed on different servers) and creates parities for redundancy. In the event of failures, we can use chunk data and parities to reconstruct the data. Let’s take a look at a concrete example (4 + 2 erasure coding) as shown in Figure 1.

*   Data is broken up into four even-sized data chunks d1, d2, d3, and d4.

*   The mathematical formula is used to calculate the parities p1 and p2. To give a much simplified example, p1 = d1 + 2\*d2 - d3 + 4\*d4 and p2 = -d1 + 5\*d2 + d3 - 3\*d4.

*   Data d3 and d4 are lost due to node crashes.

*   The mathematical formula is used to reconstruct lost data d3 and d4, using the known values of d1, d2, p1, and p2.

How much extra space does erasure coding need? For every two chunks of data, we need one parity block, so the storage overhead is 50% (Figure 2). While in 3-copy replication, the storage overhead is 200% (Figure 2).

title: Explaining JSON Web Token (JWT) to a 10 Year Old Kid
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explaining JSON Web Token (JWT) in simple terms for kids.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
Imagine you have a special box called a JWT. Inside this box, there are three parts: a header, a payload, and a signature.

The header is like the label on the outside of the box. It tells us what type of box it is and how it's secured. It's usually written in a format called JSON, which is just a way to organize information using curly braces { } and colons :

The payload is like the actual message or information you want to send. It could be your name, age, or any other data you want to share. It's also written in JSON format, so it's easy to understand and work with.

Now, the signature is what makes the JWT secure. It's like a special seal that only the sender knows how to create. The signature is created using a secret code, kind of like a password. This signature ensures that nobody can tamper with the contents of the JWT without the sender knowing about it.

When you want to send the JWT to a server, you put the header, payload, and signature inside the box. Then you send it over to the server. The server can easily read the header and payload to understand who you are and what you want to do.

title: How Big Keys Impact Redis Persistence
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore the impact of large keys on Redis AOF persistence modes.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
We call a key that contains a large size of data a big key. For example, the size of the key is 5 MB.

The diagram shows how big keys impact Redis AOF (Append-Only-File) persistence.

There are three modes when we turn on AOF persistence:

*   Always - synchronously write data to the disk whenever there is a data update in memory.

*   EverySec - write to the disk every second.

*   No - Redis doesn’t control when the data is written to the disk. Instead, the operating system decides when the data is written to the disk.

How do we analyze the impact of big keys?

Redis writes keys into memory first, then calls write() to write the data into the kernel buffer cache. Then fsync() flushes all modified in-core data of the file to the disk device. There are 3 modes.

In “Always” mode, it calls fsync() synchronously. If we need to update a big key, the main thread will be blocked because it has to wait for the write to complete.

“EveySec” starts a background timer task to call fsync() every second, so big keys have no impact on the Redis main thread.

“No” mode never calls fsync(). It is up to the operating system. Big keys have no impact on the main thread.

title: Designing a Permission System
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore common permission system designs: ACL, DAC, MAC, ABAC, and RBAC.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
The diagram below lists 5 common ways.

1. ACL (Access Control List)

ACL is a list of rules that specifies which users are granted or denied access to a particular resource.

*   Pros - Easy to understand.
*   Cons - error-prone, maintenance cost is high

2. DAC (Discretionary Access Control)

This is based on ACL. It grants or restricts object access via an access policy determined by an object's owner group.

*   Pros - Easy and flexible. Linux file system supports DAC.
*   Cons - Scattered permission control, too much power for the object’s owner group.

3. MAC (Mandatory Access Control)

Both resource owners and resources have classification labels. Different labels are granted with different permissions.

*   Pros - strict and straightforward.
*   Cons - not flexible.

4. ABAC (Attribute-based access control)

Evaluate permissions based on attributes of the Resource owner, Action, Resource, and Environment.

*   Pros - flexible
*   Cons - the rules can be complicated, and the implementation is hard. It is not commonly used.

5. RBAC (Role-based Access Control)

Evaluate permissions based on roles

*   Pros - flexible in assigning roles.

Cache Aside

When an application needs to access data, it first checks the cache. If the data is not present (a cache miss), it fetches the data from the data store, stores it in the cache, and then returns the data to the user. This pattern is particularly useful for scenarios where data is read frequently but updated less often.

Materialized View

A Materialized View is a database object that contains the results of a query. It is physically stored, meaning the data is actually computed and stored on disk, as opposed to being dynamically generated upon each request. This can significantly speed up query times for complex calculations or aggregations that would otherwise need to be computed on the fly. title: Retry Strategies for System Failures
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore retry strategies for handling transient errors in distributed systems.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
In distributed systems and networked applications, retry strategies are crucial for handling transient errors and network instability effectively. The diagram shows 4 common retry strategies.

Linear Backoff

Linear backoff involves waiting for a progressively increasing fixed interval between retry attempts.

*   Advantages: Simple to implement and understand.

*   Disadvantages: May not be ideal under high load or in high-concurrency environments as it could lead to resource contention or "retry storms".

Linear Jitter Backoff

Linear jitter backoff modifies the linear backoff strategy by introducing randomness to the retry intervals. This strategy still increases the delay linearly but adds a random "jitter" to each interval.

*   Advantages: The randomness helps spread out the retry attempts over time, reducing the chance of synchronized retries across instances.

*   Disadvantages: Although better than simple linear backoff, this strategy might still lead to potential issues with synchronized retries as the base interval increases only linearly.

Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff involves increasing the delay between retries exponentially. The interval might start at 1

title: How does Garbage Collection work?
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore how garbage collection reclaims unused memory automatically.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
Garbage collection is an automatic memory management feature used in programming languages to reclaim memory no longer used by the program.

Java

Java provides several garbage collectors, each suited for different use cases:

*   Serial Garbage Collector: Best for single-threaded environments or small applications.

*   Parallel Garbage Collector: Also known as the "Throughput Collector."

*   CMS (Concurrent Mark-Sweep) Garbage Collector: Low-latency collector aiming to minimize pause times.

*   G1 (Garbage-First) Garbage Collector: Aims to balance throughput and latency.

*   Z Garbage Collector (ZGC): A low-latency garbage collector designed for applications that require large heap sizes and minimal pause times.

Python

Python's garbage collection is based on reference counting and a cyclic garbage collector:

*   Reference Counting: Each object has a reference count; when it reaches zero, the memory is freed.

*   Cyclic Garbage Collector: Handles circular references that can't be resolved by reference counting.

GoLang

Concurrent Mark-and-Sweep Garbage Collector: Go's garbage collector operates concurrently with the application, minimizing stop-the-world pauses.

title: How Does Redis Persist Data?
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore Redis data persistence: AOF, RDB, and mixed approaches.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
Redis is an in-memory database. If the server goes down, the data will be lost.

The diagram above shows two ways to persist Redis data on disk:

1. AOF (Append-Only File)
2. RDB (Redis Database)

Note that data persistence is not performed on the critical path and doesn't block the write process in Redis.

AOF (Append-Only File)

Unlike a write-ahead log, the Redis AOF log is a write-after log. Redis executes commands to modify the data in memory first and then writes it to the log file. AOF log records the commands instead of the data. The event-based design simplifies data recovery. Additionally, AOF records commands after the command has been executed in memory, so it does not block the current write operation.

RDB (Redis Database)

The restriction of AOF is that it persists commands instead of data. When we use the AOF log for recovery, the whole log must be scanned. When the size of the log is large, Redis takes a long time to recover. So Redis provides another way to persist data - RDB.

RDB records snapshots of data at specific points in time. When the server needs to be recovered, the data snapshot can be directly loaded into memory for fast recovery.

SSH (Secure Shell) is a network protocol used to securely connect to remote machines over an unsecured network. It encrypts the connection and provides various mechanisms for authentication and data transfer.

SSH has two versions: SSH-1 and SSH-2. SSH-2 was standardized by the IETF.

It has three main layers: Transport Layer, Authentication Layer, and Connection Layer.

Transport Layer

The Transport Layer provides encryption, integrity, and data protection to ensure secure communication between the client and server.

Authentication Layer

The Authentication Layer verifies the identity of the client to ensure that only authorized users can access the server.

Connection Layer

The Connection Layer multiplexes the encrypted and authenticated communication into multiple logical channels.

title: Data Transmission Between Applications
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore how data travels between applications in detail.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
The diagram below shows how a server sends data to another server.

Assume a chat application running in the user space sends out a chat message. The message is sent to the send buffer in the kernel space. The data then goes through the network stack and is wrapped with a TCP header, an IP header, and a MAC header. The data also goes through qdisc (Queueing Disciplines) for flow control. Then the data is sent to the NIC (Network Interface Card) via a ring buffer.

The data is sent to the internet via NIC. After many hops among routers and switches, the data arrives at the NIC of the receiving server.

The NIC of the receiving server puts the data in the ring buffer and sends a hard interrupt to the CPU. The CPU sends a soft interrupt so that ksoftirqd receives data from the ring buffer. Then the data is unwrapped through the data link layer, network layer and transport layer. Eventually, the data (chat message) is copied to the user space and reaches the chat application on the receiving side.

title: How NAT Enabled the Internet
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore how NAT facilitated the expansion of the internet.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
Network Address Translation (NAT) is the process that has made the growth of the Internet possible.

But how does it work?

1. In a corporate or home setting, multiple devices (phones, computers, etc.) share one router with a single public IP address.
2. When a device wants to access the internet, it sends a request to your router. The request contains the device's private IP address.
3. The router’s NAT process replaces the private IP with the router’s public IP.
4. The modified request is sent to the internet.
5. When the response comes back, NAT checks its record and replaces the public IP with the correct private IP. It sends the response to the right device.

NAT has several important uses:

*   Conserves public IP addresses: Without NAT, IPv4 addresses would have been depleted much faster, severely limiting the growth of the Internet.
*   Allows sharing: It allows sharing a single public IP address across multiple devices.

2013 - Persistence

2015 - Cluster

Multi-Service Deployment

In this model, we deploy new changes to multiple services simultaneously. This approach is easy to implement. But since all the services are upgraded at the same time, it is hard to manage and test dependencies. It’s also hard to rollback safely.

Blue-Green Deployment

With blue-green deployment, we have two identical environments: one is staging (blue) and the other is production (green). The staging environment is one version ahead of production. Once testing is done in the staging environment, user traffic is switched to the staging environment, and the staging becomes the production. This deployment strategy is simple to perform rollback, but having two identical production quality environments could be expensive.

Canary Deployment

A canary deployment upgrades services gradually, each time to a subset of users. It is cheaper than blue-green deployment and easy to perform rollback. *   For 4XX HTTP error code, do not retry.

title: Storing Passwords Safely: A Comprehensive Guide

Things NOT to do

*   Storing passwords in plain text is not a good idea because anyone with internal access can see them.

*   Storing password hashes directly is not sufficient because it is prone to precomputation attacks, such as rainbow tables.

*   To mitigate precomputation attacks, we salt the passwords.

What is salt?

According to OWASP guidelines, “a salt is a unique, randomly generated string that is added to each password as part of the hashing process”.

How to store a password and salt?

1.  A salt is not meant to be secret and it can be stored in plain text in the database. It is used to ensure the hash result is unique to each password.

2.  The password can be stored in the database using the following format: 𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘩( 𝘱𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘥 + 𝘴𝘢𝘭𝘵).

How to validate a password?

To validate a password, it can go through the following process:

1.  A client enters the password.

2.  The system fetches the corresponding salt from the database.

3.  The system appends the salt to the password and hashes it. Let’s call the hashed value H1.

4.  The system compares H1 and H2, where H2 is the hash stored in the database. If they are the same, the password is valid.

*   Failover: Routes traffic to a primary endpoint but automatically switches to a secondary endpoint if the primary is unavailable.
*   Geolocation: Distributes traffic based on the geographic location of the requester, aiming to provide localized content or services.
*   Latency: Directs traffic to the endpoint that provides the lowest latency for the requester, enhancing user experience with faster response times.
*   Multivalue Answer: Responds to DNS queries with multiple IP addresses, allowing the client to select an endpoint. However, it should not be considered a replacement for a load balancer.
*   Weighted Routing Policy: Distributes traffic across multiple endpoints with assigned weights, allowing for proportional traffic distribution based on these weights.

title: IPv4 vs. IPv6: Differences
prompt: Look at the diagram and explain: Explore the key differences between IPv4 and IPv6 protocols.. What are the key concepts shown?
answer:
The transition from Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) to Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) is primarily driven by the need for more internet addresses, alongside the desire to streamline certain aspects of network management.

Format and Length

IPv4 uses a 32-bit address format, which is typically displayed as four decimal numbers separated by dots (e.g., 192.168.0.12). The 32-bit format allows for approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses, a number that is rapidly proving insufficient due to the explosion of internet-connected devices.

In contrast, IPv6 utilizes a 128-bit address format, represented by eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons (e.g., 50B3:F200:0211:AB00:0123:4321:6571:B000). This expansion allows for approximately much more addresses, ensuring the internet's growth can continue unabated.

Header

The IPv4 header is more complex and includes fields such as the header length, service type, total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, time to live (TTL), protocol, header checksum, source and destination IP addresses, and options.

IPv6 headers are designed to be simpler and more efficient. The fixed header size is 40 bytes and includes
